en: Netti:
The Section on Detailed Exposition, Part One:
Concordance (Sampāta) 1
The Convergence of the Modes of Exposition:
“First, having surveyed the directions by means of the ‘surveying of the directions,’ there are sixteen modes.”
“Having condensed it, one should point out the Sutta by means of the hook and the three methods.
Where is its exposition to be found when thus stated?
In the sequence of the sustenance of the teaching (*desanāhārasampāta*). Therein, what is the sequence of the sustenance of the teaching?
"With an unguarded mind..."
And by one struck down by wrong view,
overcome by sloth and torpor,
one goes under the power of Māra.”
By "with an unguarded mind," what does he teach? That negligence is the domain of death.
By "struck by wrong view": that which is called "struck by wrong view" occurs when one perceives the impermanent as permanent; that is a perversion (*vipallāsa*).
What, then, is the characteristic of that perversion?
Perversion (vipallāsa) has the characteristic of grasping in a distorted way. What does it pervert?
It perverts three things: perception, mind, and view.
So, where does it distort?
It distorts with respect to the four bases of selfhood: one regards form as self, or self as possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form.
Likewise regarding feeling... [and so on].
One regards perception as self... [and so on] ... volitional formations as self...
consciousness as self; or one regards self as possessing consciousness, or consciousness as being in self, or self as being in consciousness.
Therein, form is the first basis for perversion: "the beautiful in the ugly.
Feeling is the second basis for perversion: "pleasure in the painful.
Perception and mental formations are the third basis for perversion: "self in the non-self."
Consciousness is the fourth basis for perversion: [the perception] "in the impermanent, there is the permanent.
There are two things that defile the mind:
craving and ignorance.
A mind shrouded by craving is distorted by two perversions: it perceives "the beautiful" in the ugly and "pleasure" in suffering.
A mind shrouded by views is distorted by two perversions: it perceives "the permanent" in the impermanent and "self" in what is not-self.
In this regard, that which is the perversion of views regards past form as self.
Past feeling … past perception,
past volitional formations …
One regards past consciousness as self.
In that regard, whatever perversion of craving there is, one delights in future form, and one delights in future feeling... [and so on].
One delights in future perception,
future volitional formations,
and future consciousness.
There are two defilements of the mind:
craving and ignorance.
When purified of these, the mind becomes pure.
For those who are hindered by ignorance and fettered by craving, as they run on and wander through the cycle of existence—
now to hell, now to the animal realm, now to the sphere of hungry ghosts, now to the host of asuras,
now among devas, and now among humans— their prior limit is not known.
"Overcome by sloth and torpor":
sloth (*thina*) is that unwieldiness and lack of serviceability of the mind;
torpor (*middha*) is that sluggishness of the body.
"He falls under the power of Māra" means he falls under the power of both the defilement-māra and the being-māra; for he is shrouded and turned toward the cycle of existence (saṃsāra).
These two truths—suffering and its origin—were taught by the Blessed One.
For their full understanding and abandonment, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma: for the full understanding of suffering and for the abandonment of its origin.
That by which one fully understands and that by which one abandons is the path.
That which is the abandoning of craving and ignorance is cessation.
These are the four truths.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “With an unguarded mind.
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said: “By way of gratification and danger.
The section on the presentation of the nutriment of teaching is concluded.
